Description
When trying to call jnp.ravel() on a dynamically shaped array when jitting, an error is raised, suggesting a pytree mismatch:
import jax
from jax import numpy as jnp

jax.config.update("jax_dynamic_shapes", True)

@jax.jit
def foo(N: int):
    arr = jnp.arange(N)   # fine if `arr = jnp.arange(5)`, i.e. fine if array is statically shaped
    raveled = arr.ravel()
    return raveled

print(foo(5))
jax.errors.SimplifiedTraceback: For simplicity, JAX has removed its internal frames from the traceback of the following exception. Set JAX_TRACEBACK_FILTERING=off to include these.

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "path/to/my/main/script.py", line 12, in <module>
    print(foo(5))
  File "path/to/my/main/script.py", line 9, in foo
    raveled = arr.ravel()
  File "path/to/my/env/lib/python3.10/site-packages/jax/_src/numpy/array_methods.py", line 745, in meth
    return getattr(self.aval, name).fun(self, *args, **kwargs)
ValueError: Too many leaves for PyTreeDef; expected 1.

After some investigation, I discovered that the bug likely lies during the making of jaxpr, during partial evaluation:
jax/jax/_src/interpreters/partial_eval.py

def trace_to_subjaxpr_dynamic2(
    fun: lu.WrappedFun, main: core.MainTrace,
    debug_info: DebugInfo | None = None
) -> tuple[Jaxpr, OutputType, list[Any]]:
  in_avals, keep_inputs = unzip2(fun.in_type)
  frame = JaxprStackFrame()
  frame.debug_info = debug_info
  with extend_jaxpr_stack(main, frame), source_info_util.reset_name_stack():
    trace = DynamicJaxprTrace(main, core.cur_sublevel())
    in_tracers = _input_type_to_tracers(trace.new_arg, in_avals)
    in_tracers_ = [t for t, keep in zip(in_tracers, keep_inputs) if keep]
    ans = fun.call_wrapped(*in_tracers_)
    out_tracers = map(trace.full_raise, ans)
    jaxpr, out_type, consts = frame.to_jaxpr2(out_tracers)
    breakpoint()  # break here after producing jaxpr
    del fun, main, trace, frame, in_tracers, out_tracers, ans
  return jaxpr, out_type, consts
> /path/to/my/env/lib/python3.10/site-packages/jax/_src/interpreters/partial_eval.py(2381)trace_to_subjaxpr_dynamic2()
-> del fun, main, trace, frame, in_tracers, out_tracers, ans
(Pdb) fun
Wrapped function:
0   : _argnums_partial   ((0,), ())
1   : flatten_fun   (PyTreeDef(((*,), {})),)
2   : _argnames_partial   (<jax._src.util.WrapKwArgs object at 0x7d674b681090>,)
3   : _argnums_partial   ((0,), ())
4   : result_paths   ()
Core: ravel

(Pdb) out_tracers
[Traced<i32[Traced<ShapedArray(int32[], weak_type=True)>with<DynamicJaxprTrace(level=2/0)>]>with<DynamicJaxprTrace(level=2/0)>]
(Pdb) out_type
((ShapedArray(int32[], weak_type=True), False), (i32[OutDBIdx(val=0)], True))
(Pdb) jaxpr
{ lambda ; a:i32[] b:i32[a]. let
    c:i32[] = mul 1 a
    d:i32[c] = reshape[dimensions=None new_sizes=(None,)] b c
  in (c, d) }

We see that, when pjitting the ravel() function, although only one output tracer is requested in out_tracers, the jaxpr and the out_type still registers two output values, both the array and the size of the dynamic dimension.
Likely, this is what leads to a pytree output mismatch for the call jaxpr later. With static shape this error is not encountered because there is no value for the dynamic dimension to return in the first place, so this is not a problem.
I noticed this function is old and no longer there in jax/jax/_src/interpreters/partial_eval.py; nevertheless, I wanted to raise this issue to see if the problem is still there.
(Update: the same error persists on latest jax and jaxlib version(0.5.3))
This bug affects everything that calls ravel() in its path, e.g. jnp.roll() without an axis specified.
System info (python version, jaxlib version, accelerator, etc.)
jax:    0.4.28
jaxlib: 0.4.28
numpy:  1.26.4
python: 3.10.12 (main, Feb  4 2025, 14:57:36) [GCC 11.4.0]
jax.devices (1 total, 1 local): [CpuDevice(id=0)]
process_count: 1
platform: uname_result(system='Linux', node='L7450-H298SW3', release='6.8.0-57-generic', version='#59~22.04.1-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Wed Mar 19 17:07:41 UTC 2', machine='x86_64')

nodes.bodyText:
Functions in jax.random currently expose "RNG implementations," sometimes abbreviated "impls," to callers. For instance, jax.random.key accepts an optional impl argument, specifying the implementation to use. At the same time, key arrays have dtypes that encode/carry this impl. In other words, there is a 1-1 correspondence between key impls and key dtypes.
Because dtypes are more familiar and must be exposed anyway (e.g. via my_array.dtype), we could build our entire API around dtypes and avoid bother callers with the notion of impls altogether.
Namely, we can:

Expose RNG dtypes (outside of the dtype attribute on arrays only), e.g. via a function jax.random.key_dtype or via individual symbols like jax.random.threefry2x32_dtype.
Change APIs that accept impl objects to accept these dtypes instead.
Deprecate and eventually remove jax.random.key_impl, since key_impl(arr) becomes redundant with arr.dtype.
nodes.title: build RNG APIs on dtypes rather than "impls"

Description
Consider the following code where we define a wrapper that swaps the arguments of a function. If we invoke this wrapper on the result of jax.jit, then calling .lower bypasses the wrapper, and essentially lowers the unwrapped function my_fun:
def swap_args_wrapper(fun: Callable):
  @functools.wraps(fun)
  def wrapped(x, y):
    return fun(y, x)
  return wrapped

@ Note the order of the decorators!
@swap_args_wrapper
@jax.jit
def my_fun(x, y):
  return x

res = my_fun(0, 1)  # Uses the decorator
res_aot = my_fun.lower(0, 1).compile()(0, 1)  # Does not use the decorator
assert np.allclose(res, res_aot)  # Fails

Note that if we swap the decorators @swap_args_wrapper and jax.jit then we get the expected result.
This happens because jax.jit produces a function with attributes .trace and .lower and when we call @swap_args_wrapper on the result, it will just copy the .trace and .lower attributes (this is what @functools.wraps does) whose values are closures that reference my_fun (without the wrapper).

Description
In order to make JAX behavior deterministic on GPUs, the recommend solution is to use XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_deterministic_ops=true. However, with jax 0.5.3, jaxlib 0.5.3, this breaks simple indexing behavior.
For example,
import os
os.environ["XLA_FLAGS"] = ""
import jax.numpy as jnp

arr = jnp.array([1, 2, 0, 0])
positions = jnp.arange(arr.shape[0])
new_arr = jnp.zeros_like(arr)
new_arr = new_arr.at[positions].set(arr)
print(new_arr)

prints the expected [1 2 0 0], while setting the xla_gpu_deterministic_ops flag to true as
import os
os.environ["XLA_FLAGS"] = "--xla_gpu_deterministic_ops=true"
import jax.numpy as jnp

arr = jnp.array([1, 2, 0, 0])
positions = jnp.arange(arr.shape[0])
new_arr = jnp.zeros_like(arr)
new_arr = new_arr.at[positions].set(arr)
print(new_arr)

returns [0, 2, 0, 0].
This issue is potentially related to the issue # 26836.

Description
Summary
This code uses jax.remat to wrap a lax.scan block and reduce memory usage during reverse-mode autodiff. It works correctly on jax==0.4.13, but fails with an OOM (out-of-memory) error on jax==0.5.3, suggesting that rematerialization no longer reduces memory as expected.
Reproducible Example
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax import lax, value_and_grad

@jax.remat
def step_fn(carry, x_t):
    x0, params = carry
    a = jnp.sin(params * x0)
    b = jnp.cos(params * a)
    out = x0 + a + b   # broadcast add to (30000, 100)
    return (out, params), None

@jax.jit
def remat_scan_f_2(params):
    carry = (init_x, params)
    for ii in range(num_blocks):
        indices = jnp.arange(ii * block_size + 1, (ii + 1) * block_size + 1)
        carry, _ = jax.remat(lambda c: lax.scan(step_fn, c, indices))(carry)
    return jnp.sum(carry[0])

block_size = 1000
total_steps = 10000
num_blocks = total_steps // block_size

params = 0.8
init_x = jax.random.normal(jax.random.PRNGKey(0), (30000, 100))

# Run with gradient
ce = value_and_grad(remat_scan_f_2)(params)


Behavior
✅ JAX 0.4.13: Code runs fine. Gradients computed without exceeding memory.

❌ JAX 0.5.3: Fails with OOM on GPU even with remat. XLA logs suggest rematerialization fails to reduce memory use.

2025-04-04 14:50:31.951485: W external/xla/xla/hlo/transforms/simplifiers/hlo_rematerialization.cc:3021] Can't reduce memory use below 27.95GiB (30014254111 bytes) by rematerialization; only reduced to 111.79GiB (120036055240 bytes), down from 111.79GiB (120036055240 bytes) originally
2025-04-04 14:50:42.613817: W external/xla/xla/tsl/framework/bfc_allocator.cc:501] Allocator (GPU_0_bfc) ran out of memory trying to allocate 111.79GiB (rounded to 120036065792)requested by op 
2025-04-04 14:50:42.614336: W external/xla/xla/tsl/framework/bfc_allocator.cc:512] *___________________________________________________________________________________________________
E0404 14:50:42.614364 3758804 pjrt_stream_executor_client.cc:3077] Execution of replica 0 failed: RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: Out of memory while trying to allocate 120036065744 bytes. [tf-allocator-allocation-error='']

JAX version: 0.4.13
JAX backend platform: gpu

Description
Summary
I am working on a project which is a compiler frontend and which uses PJRT to hook to a custom MLIR compiler which hooks to a custom backend and finally down to custom Tenstorrent HW.
Running cmake build in our project we end up with build/src/tt/pjrt_plugin_tt.so. Registering that plugin the usual xla_bridge way works properly and we have a bunch of jax ops and even NN models written in jax that work just fine.
Now, this .so file is what I am trying to pack into a wheel so that it can be easily distributed to anyone wishing to use jax with TT HW.
Details
This is my setup.py
# ... custom class to build the project ...

setup(
    name=metadata.project_name,
    version=metadata.version,
    install_requires=metadata.requirements,
    classifiers=[
        "License :: Apache-2.0",
        "Programming Language :: Python :: 3",
    ],
    cmdclass={
        "bdist_wheel": BdistWheel,
        "build_py": CMakeBuildPy,
    },
    package_dir={
        "jax_plugins.pjrt_plugin_tt": "jax_plugins/pjrt_plugin_tt",
        "pjrt_plugin_tt": "build/src/tt/",
    },
    packages=[
        "jax_plugins.pjrt_plugin_tt",
        "pjrt_plugin_tt",
    ],
    package_data={
        "pjrt_plugin_tt": ["pjrt_plugin_tt.so"],
    },
    entry_points={
        "jax_plugins": [
            "pjrt_plugin_tt = jax_plugins.pjrt_plugin_tt",
        ],
    },
    long_description=metadata.description,
    long_description_content_type=metadata.description_content_type,
    zip_safe=metadata.zip_safe,
)
and this is jax_plugins/pjrt_plugin_tt/__init__.py
import os
import jax
import jax._src.xla_bridge as xb


def initialize():
    import pjrt_plugin_tt

    pjrt_plugin_parent_dir = list(pjrt_plugin_tt.__path__)[0]
    plugin_path = os.path.join(pjrt_plugin_parent_dir, "pjrt_plugin_tt.so")

    if not os.path.exists(plugin_path):
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            f"ERROR: Native library {plugin_path} does not exist. "
            f"This most likely indicates an issue with how {__package__} "
            f"was built or installed."
        )

    xb.register_plugin(
        "tt",
        priority=500,
        library_path=plugin_path,
        options=None,
    )

    jax.config.update("jax_platforms", "tt")
This builds wheel just fine.
Testing the wheel distribution
I copy the wheel over to a new folder with a brand new venv. So now I only have
(env) work/test_wheel$ ls
env  pjrt_plugin_tt-250404+main.c8c5b68-py3-none-linux_x86_64.whl

env/lib/python3.10/site-packages/pjrt_plugin_tt/pjrt_plugin_tt.so

jax.numpy.__array_namespace_info__().default_device() returns None.
It should return a Device object (read data-apis/array-api#835 for controversy on which device should be returned).
jax.numpy.__array_namespace_info__().devices() is an alias to jax.devices().
While this is not explicitly spelled out by the Array API (https://data-apis.org/array-api/latest/API_specification/generated/array_api.info.devices.html#devices), I believe it is misleading as it lacks the backend optional parameter that jax.devices offers. I think it should return a list of all devices available at the moment of calling it; e.g. when CUDA is available, it should return [CpuDevice(id=0), CudaDevice(id=0)].

nodes.bodyText:
Hi JAX team and @sharadmv,
I found an unnecessary constraint in the flash_attention_kernel implementation in the Splash Attention module that prevents small models from using it.
Currently, the kernel enforces that head_dim_v must be a multiple of NUM_LANES (128):
head_dim_v_repeats, rem = divmod(head_dim_v, NUM_LANES)
if rem != 0:
    raise NotImplementedError(
        f"{head_dim_v=} should be a multiple of {NUM_LANES}"
    )
Source:

  
    
      jax/jax/experimental/pallas/ops/tpu/splash_attention/splash_attention_kernel.py
    
    
        Lines 714 to 718
      in
      49aad1b
    
  
  
    

        
          
           head_dim_v_repeats, rem = divmod(head_dim_v, NUM_LANES) 
        

        
          
           if rem != 0: 
        

        
          
             raise NotImplementedError( 
        

        
          
                 f"{head_dim_v=} should be a multiple of {NUM_LANES}" 
        

        
          
             ) 
        
    
  


However, this constraint is unnecessary. It arises from the way head_dim_v_repeats is used to reshape alpha:
alpha_o = pltpu.repeat(alpha, head_dim_v_repeats, axis=1)
This reshape assumes alpha has shape [bq, NUM_LANES] and change it to [bq, head_dim]. However in fact, alpha is $(d_{i-1}' * e^{m_{i-1} - m_i}) / d_i$ in Algorithm FlashAttention (Tiling) and it should have shape [bq, 1], not [bq, NUM_LANES].
In the code:


$m_i$ corresponds to m_scratch


$d_i'$ corresponds to l_scratch


Currently, both are unnecessarily allocated with shape [bq, NUM_LANES], causing all NUM_LANES elements to redundantly store the same value.
Source:

  
    
      jax/jax/experimental/pallas/ops/tpu/splash_attention/splash_attention_kernel.py
    
    
        Lines 1056 to 1057
      in
      49aad1b
    
  
  
    

        
          
           jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((bq, NUM_LANES), jnp.float32),  # m_scratch 
        

        
          
           jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((bq, NUM_LANES), jnp.float32),  # l_scratch 
        
    
  


To be clear, let me annotate the shape in the Flash attention algorithm in https://courses.cs.washington.edu/courses/cse599m/23sp/notes/flashattn.pdf


Why this matters
By changing the shape of m_scratch, l_scratch, and alpha to [bq, 1]:

We avoid unnecessary memory and compute overhead.
We eliminate the need to repeat(alpha, head_dim_v_repeats, ...).
Most importantly, we can remove the head_dim_v % NUM_LANES == 0 constraint entirely.

This enables smaller models (e.g. sLLMs) to use Splash Attention.

Unfortunately, due to my company's internal policy, I’m unable to submit a PR myself. I hope the JAX maintainers can address this issue — fixing it should not require major changes and will benefit a wider range of users.
Thanks for your excellent work!
nodes.title: [Splash Attention] Remove unnecessary `head_dim_v % NUM_LANES == 0` constraint

Description
I found that the output of a jitted version of a function can differ significantly from the unjitted version's output.
Here is a minimal code to reproduce the issue.
import jax
from jax import numpy as jnp

def forward(x, emb, w, b, y):
    x = x + emb[:, :x.shape[1]]
    x = jnp.dot(x, w) + b
    return jnp.mean((x - y) ** 2)

jax_jitted_forward = jax.jit(forward)


in_dim = 32
key = jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
batch_size, seq_len = 2, 3

x = jax.random.normal(key, (batch_size, seq_len, in_dim))
y = jax.random.normal(key, (batch_size, seq_len, in_dim))

weights = jax.random.normal(key, (in_dim, in_dim))
bias = jax.random.normal(key, (in_dim,))

def get_position_angle_vec(position):
    return [position / jnp.power(10000, 2 * (hid_j // 2) / in_dim) for hid_j in range(in_dim)]

emb = jnp.array([get_position_angle_vec(pos_i) for pos_i in range(30)])
emb = emb.at[:, 0::2].set(jnp.sin(emb[:, 0::2]))
emb = emb.at[:, 1::2].set(jnp.cos(emb[:, 1::2]))
emb = emb[None, ...]

print("forward:", forward(x, emb, weights, bias, y))
print("jax_jitted_forward:", jax_jitted_forward(x, emb, weights, bias, y))

Description
I am getting the following error:
jaxlib.xla_extension.XlaRuntimeError: INTERNAL: ptxas exited with non-zero error code 65280, output: ptxas error   : Entry function 'input_concatenate_reduce_subtract_fusion' uses too much shared data (0xc180 bytes, 0xc000 max)
Reproducibility
I sadly couldn't simplify the code to minimal reproducibility, but the error can be reproduced by:

Checking out the following branch: https://github.com/p-doom/reward-redistribution/tree/franz/ptxas-error-example
Installing the dependencies: pip install -e .
Running the following:

python3 stoix/systems/ppo/anakin/ff_ppo.py env=navix/four_rooms_7x7 system.redistribute_reward=false system.disable_autoreset=false env.kwargs.disable_autoreset=false
Error source
The error itself is pretty self-descriptive. XLA seems to fuse too many operations at once, which leads to the GPU running out of shared memory. However, this only happens if a jax.debug.breakpoint is set (see https://github.com/p-doom/reward-redistribution/blob/66e949d2a2091543dc6003e05158a9af3453f8d1/stoix/systems/ppo/anakin/ff_ppo.py#L144), which is why I am opening an issue in the JAX repository instead of the XLA one. If this is not a JAX issue, feel free to point me to XLA.
Quickfixes
I implemented two (repository-level) quickfixes for this error in the following two PRs:

p-doom/reward-redistribution#9
p-doom/reward-redistribution#13

Additional pointers
Here are some pointers that may or may not be useful:

#3122

Description
Hi there!
When using jax.random.choice with replace=False and a weights array p I get pretty poor performance compared to torch.
Upon digging deeper I saw the following code:

  
    
      jax/jax/_src/random.py
    
    
        Lines 672 to 674
      in
      074216e
    
  
  
    

        
          
           # Gumbel top-k trick: https://timvieira.github.io/blog/post/2019/09/16/algorithms-for-sampling-without-replacement/ 
        

        
          
           g = -gumbel(key, (n_inputs,), dtype=p_arr.dtype) - jnp.log(p_arr) 
        

        
          
           ind = jnp.argsort(g)[:n_draws] 
        
    
  


As mentioned in the code, this is using the Gumbel top-k trick. However, I notice that the implementation using
ind = jnp.argsort(g)[:n_draws]
which is in my opinion a very inefficient way of selecting the top k elements, as it involves sorting a possibly huge array unnecessarily.
When using instead
g = -gumbel(key, (n_inputs,), dtype=p_arr.dtype) - jnp.log(p_arr)
ind = lax.top_k(-g, k=n_draws)[1]
... I get up to 35x speedups depending on the size of the array 😅 Please let me know if I'm overlooking something here, but it seems to me lax.top_k is much better optimized and a natural fit.
Here's how I'm testing this
import jax.random
from timeit import default_timer as timer

B = 16
rng = jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
for N in [1000, 1_000_000, 10_000_000]:
    p = jax.random.uniform(rng, (N,))
    ts = timer()
    jax.random.choice(rng, N, (B,), replace=False, p=p).block_until_ready()
    print(f'Time taken for N={N:>10,}: {timer()-ts:.4f}s')

Time taken for N=10,000,000: 3.8169s

With fix

The actual problematic line is the one below it.
Here's the annotated reduced reproducible example:

        cond = jax.lax.select(sims == max_sims, a, b)
        # NOTE: Changing this to jnp.zeros(...) avoids any error entirely.

        max_idxes = jnp.min(cond, axis=1, keepdims=True).astype(jnp.int32)

Description
Hi, I was comparing the relatively speed of three different implementations of a function and found the following result a bit... unexpected.
The function I'm using takes an input and adds a certain number of arrays to it.
I've tested three implementations using 1) a Python for loop, 2) jax.xla.fori_loop, and 3) a list comprehension.
import time
from functools import partial
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp


@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("size",))
def f_for_loop(x: float, size: int) -> jax.Array:
    out = x + jnp.zeros(size)
    for i in range(size):
        out = out + i * jnp.arange(size)
    return out


@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("size",))
def f_lax_fori(x, size):

    def body(ind, carry_on):
        return carry_on + ind * jnp.arange(size)

    return jax.lax.fori_loop(0, size, body, x + jnp.zeros(size))


@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("size",))
def f_comprehension(x, size):
    out = x + jnp.zeros(size)
    return out + sum([i * jnp.arange(size) for i in range(size)])


for x, size in [(1, 100), (1, 10_000)]:
    print(f"*** {size=} *** ")
    for func in [f_for_loop, f_lax_fori, f_comprehension]:
        print(f"---{func.__name__}---")
        t0 = time.time()
        func(x, size).block_until_ready()
        print(f"1st:\t{time.time() - t0:.2e}")

        t0 = time.time()
        func(x, size).block_until_ready()
        print(f"2nd:\t{time.time() - t0:.2e}")
To compare the results I time the functions with a given input twice: The first run (I assume) times both the lowering and run time, whereas the second one is dominated by run time.
The results (in seconds) are as follows:
*** size=100 ***
---f_for_loop---
1st:	1.40e-01
2nd:	1.14e-04
---f_lax_fori---
1st:	3.56e-02
2nd:	4.10e-05
---f_comprehension---
1st:	7.39e-02
2nd:	1.86e-04
*** size=10000 ***
---f_for_loop---
1st:	6.63e+01
2nd:	8.45e-03
---f_lax_fori---
1st:	7.74e-02
2nd:	4.15e-02
---f_comprehension---
1st:	4.03e+01
2nd:	2.16e-04

fori_loop is obviously faster to compile as the other two functions need to be unrolled by jit (hence those ~60s of compilation for size=10_000).
The thing that baffles me is that, for size=10_000 a Python list comprehension + sum is faster by a factor 190 than the fori_loop implementation.
Is this behavior expected? Am I making a mistake in my measurements?
Why does a "pure jax" implementation run so much slower?
Thanks in advance,

Description
In JAX, a 4-bit float tensor (e.g., float4_e2m1fn) is padded to 1 byte per element. However, XLA stores two 4-bit elements compactly in a single byte. As a result, jax.debug.print does not correctly display the packed tensor, leading to inconsistent output between JIT-compiled and non-JIT-compiled runs.
The issue is demonstrated in the following example, where the outputs differ depending on whether JIT compilation is used:
import jax.numpy as jnp
import jax
output_type = jnp.float32
shape = (64, 32)
k1 = jax.random.key(0)

a = jax.random.uniform(k1, shape, minval=-1.0, dtype=output_type)
a_e2m1 = a.astype(jnp.float4_e2m1fn)

print(f"py print ref:{a_e2m1}")

def fn(x):
  jax.debug.print("jax.debug.print {x}", x=x)
  return x

print("In jit-compiled")
out = jax.jit(fn)(a_e2m1)
print("Outside jit-compiled")
_ = fn(a_e2m1)

Description
When using sharding constraints on intermediate arrays in a jax.jit function, the arrays can be silently replicated along that axis, rather than sharded, if the size of the axis is not divisible by the number of devices on the axis.
Reproducing script, taking the example of embedding weights with vocab size vocab_size, on 8xGPUs:
import jax
import numpy as np
import jax.numpy as jnp

from jax.sharding import Mesh, PartitionSpec as P, NamedSharding
from jax.lax import with_sharding_constraint as shard

def main():
    vocab_size = 17 # change to 16 for correct sharding
    mesh = Mesh(np.reshape(jax.devices("gpu"), (8,)), ('data',))

    @jax.jit
    def fn():
        embedding = jnp.arange(vocab_size*16).reshape(vocab_size, 16)
        embedding = shard(embedding, P('data', None))
        jax.debug.visualize_array_sharding(embedding)
        return embedding
    
    with mesh:
        embedding = fn().block_until_ready()
    jax.debug.visualize_array_sharding(embedding)

    # uncomment to hard error when not-divisible (expected)
    # embedding = jax.device_put(embedding, NamedSharding(mesh, P('data', None))) 
    # jax.debug.visualize_array_sharding(embedding)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
When vocab_size is not divisible by 8, the array sharding visualisation will show embedding actually gets fully replicated with no error or warning. This is unexpected as the device_put function will hard error when attempting to do a similar thing.
When it is divisible by 8, it will correctly replicate the array.
The expected behaviour is to throw an error when attempting to do this type of sharding. Otherwise you could get a silent increase in the memory requirements of jit functions (eg. imagine a vocab size of >1M elements)

Description
Hi,
Not sure if this should be posted here or on XLA. I have an example where I try to train a PINN and I've run it on three systems: one with an A100 with jax==0.5.0 , one with and AMD RX 6950XT and one with an Instinct MI250X. Both AMD systems have jax==0.4.38 since it's the last official build supported by them. The reproducer is the following:
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.integrate import odeint
import optax
import time
import pandas as pd
import jaxopt
import diffrax as dfx
import jax.profiler
import os

#os.environ['XLA_FLAGS'] = ('--xla_gpu_triton_gemm_any=True')
#jax.config.update("jax_default_matmul_precision", "high")
device = jax.devices("gpu")[0] if jax.devices("gpu") else jax.devices("cpu")[0]
print(device)

# Drug model
def func_gt(t, y, args):
    A, B, C, D, E = y
    k1 = 0.05
    k2 = 0.1
    k3 = 0.01
    # Reactions
    r1 = k1 * A * B
    r2 = k2 * C
    r3 = k3 * A**2
    dcAdt = -r1-2*r3  # dA/dt
    dcBdt = -r1  # dB/dt
    dcCdt = r1 - r2  # dC/dt
    dcDdt = r3  # dD/dt
    dcEdt = 2*r2  # dE/dt
    return jnp.array([dcAdt, dcBdt, dcCdt, dcDdt, dcEdt])

@jax.jit
def get_data(y0, t_dense, t_data):
    key = jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
    # noise = 0.01
    term = dfx.ODETerm(func_gt)
    solver = dfx.Tsit5()
    t0 = t_dense[0]
    t1 = t_dense[-1]
    dt0 = 0.1
    saveat = dfx.SaveAt(ts=t_dense)
    sol = dfx.diffeqsolve(term, solver, t0, t1, dt0, y0, saveat = saveat)
    y_dense = sol.ys
    t_ind = jnp.clip(
        jnp.floor(len(t_dense) * t_data / t_dense[-1]).astype(int), 
        0, t_dense.size - 1
    )
    return y_dense, jnp.take(sol.ys, t_ind, axis=0)


def get_all_data(y0s, t_dense, t_data):
    def solve_ode(y0):
        y_dense, y_data = get_data(y0, t_dense, t_data)
        return y_dense, y_data
    y_dense_all, y_data_all = jax.vmap(solve_ode)(y0s)
    return y_dense_all.transpose(1, 2, 0), y_data_all.transpose(1, 2, 0)


def init_params(layers):
    keys = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(0), len(layers) - 1)
    params = []
    for key, n_in, n_out in zip(keys, layers[:-1], layers[1:]):
        W = jax.random.normal(key, shape=(n_in, n_out)) / jnp.sqrt(n_in)
        B = jax.random.normal(key, shape=(n_out,))
        params.append({'W': W, 'B': B})
    return params

def normalize_data(x):
    stdev = jnp.std(x, axis = (0, 2))
    avg = jnp.mean(x, axis = (0, 2))
    return avg, stdev

def fwd(params, t, ic):
    t_flat = t.reshape(-1, 1)
    ic_expanded = jnp.broadcast_to(ic, (t.shape[0], ic.shape[0]))
    X = jnp.concatenate([t_flat, ic_expanded], axis=1)
    *hidden, last = params
    for layer in hidden:
        X = jax.nn.silu(X @ layer['W'] + layer['B'])
    return X @ last['W'] + last['B']

def fwd_extra(params,y,avg,sigma):
    X = (y-avg)/sigma
    *hidden,last = params
    for layer in hidden :
        X = jax.nn.silu(X@layer['W']+layer['B'])
    X = X@last['W'] + last['B']
    return transfer_to_device(X)


@jax.jit
def MSE(true, pred):
    return jnp.mean((true - pred) ** 2)

@jax.jit
def ODE_loss(t, y, params_extra, avg, sigma):
    
    
    y_reshaped = y.transpose(0, 2, 1).reshape(-1, 5)
    derivs = fwd_extra(params_extra, y_reshaped, avg, sigma)
    derivs = derivs.reshape(y.shape[0], y.shape[2], 5).transpose(0, 2, 1)
    
    return derivs

@jax.jit
def loss_fun(params, params_extra, t_data, t_dense, t_c, ics, y_data, y_dense, avg, sigma):
    def get_predictions(ic):
        return fwd(params, t_data, ic)
    
    preds_data = jax.vmap(get_predictions)(ics).transpose(1, 2, 0)
    loss_data = MSE(y_data, preds_data)
    # Get predictions at dense points
    def get_collocation_predictions(ic):
        return fwd(params, t_c, ic)
    def get_dense_predictions(ic):
        return fwd(params, t_dense, ic)
    
    pred_collocation = jax.vmap(get_collocation_predictions)(ics).transpose(1, 2, 0)
    pred_dense = jax.vmap(get_dense_predictions)(ics).transpose(1, 2, 0)
    RHS_collocation = ODE_loss(t_c, pred_collocation, params_extra, avg, sigma)

    def get_time_derivs(ic):
        def single_pred(t):
            return fwd(params, jnp.array([t]), ic)
        
        time_derivs = jax.vmap(lambda t: jax.jacfwd(single_pred)(t).squeeze())(t_c)
        return time_derivs
    
    time_derivs = jax.vmap(get_time_derivs)(ics).transpose(1, 2, 0)
    loss_physics = MSE(time_derivs, RHS_collocation)
    t0 = jnp.array([0.0])
    preds_ic = jax.vmap(lambda ic: fwd(params, t0, ic))(ics)
    loss_ic = MSE(ics, preds_ic.squeeze())
    loss_val = MSE(y_dense, pred_dense)
    return loss_data, loss_physics, loss_ic, loss_val

@jax.jit
def loss_fun_total(params, params_extra, t_data, t_dense, t_c, ics, y_data, y_dense, loss_weight, avg, sigma):
    loss_data, loss_physics, loss_ic, _ = loss_fun(
        params, params_extra, t_data, t_dense, t_c, ics, y_data, y_dense, avg, sigma
    )
    
    return (loss_weight[0] * loss_data + 
            loss_weight[1] * loss_physics + 
            loss_weight[2] * loss_ic)

@jax.jit
def update(opt_state, opt_state_extra, params, params_extra, t_data, t_dense, t_c,
           ics, y_data, y_dense, loss_weights, avg, sigma):
    """Single optimization step"""
    loss_value, grads = jax.value_and_grad(loss_fun_total, argnums=(0, 1))(
        params, params_extra, t_data, t_dense, t_c, ics, y_data, y_dense, loss_weights, avg, sigma
    )
    updates, opt_state = optimizer.update(grads[0], opt_state)
    params = optax.apply_updates(params, updates)
    updates_extra, opt_state_extra = optimizer_ex.update(grads[1], opt_state_extra)
    params_extra = optax.apply_updates(params_extra, updates_extra)
    return loss_value, opt_state, opt_state_extra, params, params_extra

def transfer_to_device(data):
    return jax.device_put(data, device)

adam_time = []
bfgs_time = []
total_time = []


A0 = 10.
B0 = 5.
doe = 0.25
plus1 = 1 + doe
minus1 = 1 - doe
y0s_train = jnp.array([[A0, B0, 0, 0, 0],
                [A0*minus1, B0*minus1, 0, 0, 0],
                [A0*minus1, B0, 0, 0, 0],
                [A0*minus1, B0*plus1, 0, 0, 0],
                [A0, B0*minus1, 0, 0, 0],
                [A0, B0*plus1, 0, 0, 0],
                [A0*plus1, B0*minus1, 0, 0, 0],
                [A0*plus1, B0, 0, 0, 0],
                [A0*plus1, B0*plus1, 0, 0, 0]])

t_dense = jnp.linspace(0., 10., 1000)
t_data = jnp.linspace(0., 10., 10)
t_dense = transfer_to_device(t_dense)
y_dense, y_data = get_all_data(y0s_train, t_dense, t_data)
y_dense = transfer_to_device(y_dense)
y_data = transfer_to_device(y_data)
A_data = y_data[:, 0]
B_data = y_data[:, 1]
C_data = y_data[:, 2]
D_data = y_data[:, 3]
E_data = y_data[:, 4]
avg, stdev = normalize_data(y_data)
t_i = jnp.array([0.])
t_i = transfer_to_device(t_i)
IC = jnp.array([A_data[0], B_data[0], C_data[0], D_data[0], E_data[0]], ndmin=2)

params_extra = transfer_to_device(init_params([5] + [16] * 4 + [5]))
optimizer = optax.adam(1e-3)
opt_state = transfer_to_device(optimizer.init(params))

start_time = time.time()

loss_weight_phase1 = transfer_to_device([1., 1., 0., 0., 0., 0., 0.])

    opt_state, opt_state_extra, params, params_extra,

        )

Description
A Python for loop of 1000 iterations in a Pallas kernel function is painfully slow to run (~ 1 hour!). Switching to an equivalent jax.lax.fori_loop implementation is much faster (no noticeable lag). For reference, an equivalent naive JAX implementation without Pallas kernel using Python for loop takes several minutes to jit compile.
To reproduce it, change the following part of the benchmark script
https://github.com/ysngshn/jax-pallas-benchmark/blob/main/run_benchmark.py#L39-L47
    h0 = h0_ref[...]

    def _step(i, h_prev):
        idx = slice_all[:seq_dim] + (i,) + slice_all[seq_dim+1:]
        h_next = activation(x_ref[idx] + whh * h_prev)
        o_ref[idx] = h_next
        return h_next

    _ = fori_loop(0, seqlen, _step, h0)
to
    h = h0_ref[...]
    
    for i in range(seqlen):
        idx = slice_all[:seq_dim] + (i,) + slice_all[seq_dim+1:]
        h = activation(x_ref[idx] + whh * h)
        o_ref[idx] = h
in the _indrnn_elementwise_kernel Pallas kernel function and rerun the script.

The following code for computing univariate derivatives of the function $cos(x)*x$
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax.experimental import jet

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)


func = lambda x: jnp.cos(x) * x

results in the following error
TypeError: lax.mul requires arguments to have the same dtypes, got float64, int64. (Tip: jnp.multiply is a similar function that does automatic type promotion on inputs).

Modifying func = lambda x: jnp.cos(x) * x to func = lambda x: jnp.cos(x) * jnp.pow(x, 1.0) fixes the error.

Description
After upgrading from jax==0.4.38 to jax==0.5.0, my implementation of Trust Region optimization results under 64-bit precision show unexpected behavior compared to the previous version. The convergence trajectory and cost reduction are significantly worse in 64-bit mode with jax==0.5.0, while 32-bit results show less disparity.
Code Context:
Uses jax.numpy.matmul, jax.jacrev, jax.jvp, and other JAX transformations.
No code changes were made between version tests.
Ensure 64-bit is explicitly enabled: jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
A minimal reproducible example is unavailable due to the complexity of the optimization setup.
Iteration Logs (64-bit):
jax==0.5.0 (problematic):
Iteration Total nfev     Cost     Cost reduction    Step norm     Optimality    Delta  Ratio
    0         1       1.1868e+09                                   2.53e+08   4.14e+04 0.00 
    1         15      1.0962e+09     9.07e+07       3.48e+01       1.58e+08   9.84e+02 0.39 
    2         16      9.4803e+08     1.48e+08       4.23e-01       1.07e+08   4.92e+03 1.01

    4         21      4.2991e+08     1.37e+08       3.60e+00       2.17e+08   1.04e+04 0.39 
    5         22      2.0051e+08     2.29e+08       2.50e+00       3.85e+07   3.11e+04 0.83 
    6         25      1.7192e+08     2.86e+07       2.95e+00       6.46e+07   1.75e+04 0.41

jax==0.4.38 (expected):
Iteration Total nfev     Cost     Cost reduction    Step norm     Optimality    Delta  Ratio
    0         1       1.1665e+09                                   3.47e+08   5.73e+04 0.00 
    1         3       6.8074e+08     4.86e+08       1.33e+01       2.09e+08   4.30e+04 0.42 
    2         4       3.1105e+08     3.70e+08       6.97e+00       2.58e+08   6.44e+04 0.54 
    3         5       1.5729e+08     1.54e+08       9.48e+00       1.90e+08   6.44e+04 0.49

    6         8       6.4314e+06     1.75e+07       1.29e+01       1.86e+07   1.45e+05 0.73 
    7         9       5.5351e+06     8.96e+05       1.84e+01       2.78e+07   1.09e+05 0.14

It is worth noting that the initial cost also varies. The same phenomenon happens in 32-bit mode, but the optimization result affects little.

Could this relate to the new jaxlib version or XLA backend updates?

Description
Tiny numbers (float64 ~1e-313) compare as equal to zero. When added to an actual zero, they become zero.
I could reproduce this on CPU, but not on GPU.
import jax
import jax.numpy as xp
import numpy as np

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
device = jax.devices("cpu")[0]
x = xp.asarray(2.22507386e-313, dtype=xp.float64, device=device)
y = x + 0.
print(f"{jax.__version__=} {x=} {y=}")  # jax.__version__='0.5.0' x=Array(2.22507386e-313, dtype=float64) y=Array(0., dtype=float64)
assert x == 0.  # Passes
assert x == y  # Passes
np.testing.assert_allclose(y, x)  # Fails

Description
In this example I run a function containing a expm on a replicated array.
The function works fine and is automatically shared in the correct way if I use jax.jit.
But if I use shard_map, the function errors with the following message:
Exception: Scan carry input and output got mismatched replication types [None, None] and [{'i'}, {'i'}]. Please open an issue at https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/issues, and as a temporary workaround pass the check_rep=False argument to shard_map
I suspect that there is a missing function to teach how shard map should handle expm
import os

os.environ["NETKET_EXPERIMENTAL_SHARDING"] = "1"
os.environ["XLA_FLAGS"] = "--xla_force_host_platform_device_count=2"

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax.sharding import Mesh, PartitionSpec as P
from jax.experimental.shard_map import shard_map

# Run VMC optimization

N = 8
xs = jnp.ones((18, N), dtype=jnp.int32)
variables = jax.random.normal(jax.random.key(1), (N, N), jnp.complex64)


mesh = Mesh(jax.devices(), axis_names=("i"))
in_specs = (P(), P("i"),)
out_specs = P("i")

variables = jax.lax.with_sharding_constraint(
    variables, jax.sharding.PositionalSharding(jax.devices()).replicate()
)
xs = jax.lax.with_sharding_constraint(
    xs, jax.sharding.PositionalSharding(jax.devices()).reshape(-1, 1)
)

def fun(v, xs):
    # Commenting this single line below makes everything work
    v = jax.scipy.linalg.expm(v)

    v = v.sum()
    return v * xs.sum(axis=-1)


res = fun(variables, xs)
print(res.sharding)


fun_shard_map = shard_map(fun, mesh=mesh, in_specs=in_specs, out_specs=out_specs)
# this fails
res = fun_shard_map(variables, xs)
print(res.sharding)

nodes.bodyText:
tl;dr It'd be nice if there were a version of jax.vjp returning a backward function that doesn't capture the activations, so it could be jitted on its own.
Say I have a function like f below:
def g(W, x):
  return jnp.sin(jnp.dot(W, x))

def f(W1, W2, W3, x):
  x = g(W1, x)
  x = g(W2, x)
  x = g(W3, x)
  return x
and my goal is to compute the vjp wrt W{1,2,3}.
I can control rematerialization within jax.vjp(f, ...), e.g. by annotating g with @jax.checkpoint:
@jax.checkpoint  # <- new
def g(W, x):
  return jnp.sin(jnp.dot(W, x))
This works well if my entire model ends up in a single jitted function along the lines of
@jax.jit
def model(W1, W2, W3, x):
    _, bwd = jax.vjp(f, W1, W2, W3, x)
    grad1, grad2, grad3, _ = bwd(jnp.ones(W3.shape[0]))
    return grad1, grad2, grad3
Now suppose I wanted the unit of jit compilation to be g rather than the full model. (This might be useful for, say, pipeline parallelism, in which we want to compile one function for each stage, but then invoke it many times on different microbatches in ways that not readily expressible using a loop.) Hence my first step might be to simply "move" the jax.jit to g:
@jax.jit  # <- new
@jax.checkpoint
def g(W, x):
  return jnp.sin(jnp.dot(W, x))

# (no more jax.jit)
def model(W1, W2, W3, x):
    _, bwd = jax.vjp(f, W1, W2, W3, x)
    grad1, grad2, grad3, _ = bwd(jnp.ones(W3.shape[0]))
    return grad1, grad2, grad3
As one would expect, this is much slower, because the backward computation now happens in eager mode. But perhaps we can fix this by decomposing the vjp and then jitting the individual parts? Decomposing is easy enough in our example:
def model(W1, W2, W3, x):
    x, bwd1 = jax.vjp(g, W1, x)
    x, bwd2 = jax.vjp(g, W2, x)
    _, bwd3 = jax.vjp(g, W3, x)
    grad3, y = bwd3(jnp.ones(W3.shape[0]))
    grad2, y = bwd2(y)
    grad1, _ = bwd1(y)
    return grad1, grad2, grad3
... but now I'm stuck! jax.jvp returns a closure that bakes in the forward pass' activation, so it's futile to jax.jit(bwd{1,2,3}) -- we'll end up recompiling on every single invocation.
It seems that what I really want is a version of jax.jvp (dubbed fwd_and_bwd below) that does not capture the activations, and allows me to manually insert jits:
g_fwd, g_bwd = fwd_and_bwd(g)
g_fwd = jax.jit(g_fwd)
g_bwd = jax.jit(g_bwd)

def model(W1, W2, W3, x):
    x, residuals1 = g_fwd(W1, x)
    x, residuals2 = g_fwd(W2, x)
    _, residuals3 = g_fwd(W3, x)
    grad3, y = g_bwd(residuals3, jnp.ones(W3.shape[0]))
    grad2, y = g_bwd(residuals2, y)
    grad1, _ = g_bwd(residuals1, y)
    return grad1, grad2, grad3
Is there a way to express fwd_and_bwd using the public JAX API today? If not, are there good reasons not to expose one?
